en.title: Three Founding Peoples & Aboriginal Groups
en.mnemonic: Three founding peoples: Aboriginal, French, British. Three Aboriginal groups by size: First Nations (65%) > Métis (30%) > Inuit (4%). New Brunswick is the ONLY officially bilingual province.

Acadians are descendants of French colonists (p. 19), not an Aboriginal group. Mohawk are one specific First Nation.

Les Premières Nations, les Loyalistes et les Inuits
Les Métis, les Acadiens et les Québécois
fr.explanation: Le terme peuples autochtones désigne trois groupes distincts : les Premières Nations, les Inuits et les Métis.

Les Britanniques, les Allemands et les Français

en.question: Who are the Acadians?
options: Descendants of French colonists who began settling in what are now the Maritime provinces in 1604, most of whom were deported between 1755 and 1763 in the 'Great Upheaval.'
An Aboriginal nation that lived along the St. Lawrence River.
Loyalists who fled to Canada from the American Revolution.
Early French explorers who searched for the Northwest Passage.
en.explanation: Page 19: 'The Acadians are the descendants of French colonists who began settling in what are now the Maritime provinces in 1604. Between 1755 and 1763 … more than two-thirds of the Acadians were deported from their homeland.'

optionAnnotations.explanation: Page 19: 'The Acadians are the descendants of French colonists who began settling in what are now the Maritime provinces in 1604. Between 1755 and 1763 … more than two-thirds of the Acadians were deported from their homeland.'
Acadians are French in origin, not Aboriginal. Confusing the two is a common error.
Those are the Loyalists, a different group. Acadians were already in Canada more than a century before the Loyalists arrived.
Acadians were settlers, not explorers. The Northwest Passage searches are a different historical thread.

en.question: Who are the Métis?
options: A distinct Aboriginal people of mixed Aboriginal and European ancestry, the majority of whom live in the Prairie provinces, who speak their own dialect called Michif.
Descendants of French colonists who settled in the Maritime provinces starting in 1604.
Inuit people who live in the Arctic.
Loyalists who came to Canada after the American Revolution.
en.explanation: Page 18: 'The Métis are a distinct people of mixed Aboriginal and European ancestry, the majority of whom live in the Prairie provinces. They come from both French- and English-speaking backgrounds and speak their own dialect, Michif.'

optionAnnotations.explanation: Page 18: 'The Métis are a distinct people of mixed Aboriginal and European ancestry, the majority of whom live in the Prairie provinces. They come from both French- and English-speaking backgrounds and speak their own dialect, Michif.'
Those are the Acadians (p. 19), not the Métis. Acadians are part of French Canada's heritage; Métis are an Aboriginal people.
The Inuit are a separate Aboriginal group living in the Arctic — also described on p. 18. Métis are distinct from Inuit.
The Loyalists are an entirely different historical group (p. 27) — settlers loyal to the British Crown who fled north after the American Revolution. Not Aboriginal.

en.question: Who are the three founding peoples of Canada?
en.explanation: Page 16: 'To understand what it means to be Canadian, it is important to know about our three founding peoples—Aboriginal, French and British.'

optionAnnotations.explanation: Page 16: 'To understand what it means to be Canadian, it is important to know about our three founding peoples—Aboriginal, French and British.'
Spanish colonization did not extend to what became Canada. The third founding people is Aboriginal — the original inhabitants — not Spanish.
These are the three groups within Aboriginal peoples (p. 17), not the three founding peoples of Canada as a whole.

Americans are not a founding people of Canada — the United States did not exist when European settlement of Canada began. The Loyalists who fled to Canada after the American Revolution were of British origin.

en.question: Who was the 15th Governor General of Canada and a popular advocate of 'unity in diversity'?
en.explanation: Page 18: 'John Buchan, the 1st Baron Tweedsmuir, was a popular Governor General of Canada (1935-40).' His remarks about immigrant groups retaining individuality and contributing to national character are on the same page.

optionAnnotations.explanation: Page 18: 'John Buchan, the 1st Baron Tweedsmuir, was a popular Governor General of Canada (1935-40).' His remarks about immigrant groups retaining individuality and contributing to national character are on the same page.
Durham reported on the Rebellions (p. 31), but was not Governor General.
Stanley donated the Stanley Cup as Governor General in 1892 (p. 81), not the 15th GG.
Laurier was a PM, not a Governor General.

en.question: Why are Anglophones generally referred to as 'English Canadians'?
options: Because the basic way of life in English-speaking areas was established by English, Welsh, Scottish, and Irish settlers from the 1600s to the 20th century
Because all Anglophones come from England
It is a recent legal designation
Because they spoke English better than other immigrants
en.explanation: Page 20: 'The basic way of life in English-speaking areas was established by hundreds of thousands of English, Welsh, Scottish and Irish settlers, soldiers and migrants from the 1600s to the 20th century. Generations of pioneers and builders of British origins, as well as other groups, invested and endured hardship in laying the foundations of our country. This helps explain why Anglophones (English speakers) are generally referred to as English Canadians.'

optionAnnotations.explanation: Page 20: 'The basic way of life in English-speaking areas was established by hundreds of thousands of English, Welsh, Scottish and Irish settlers, soldiers and migrants from the 1600s to the 20th century. Generations of pioneers and builders of British origins, as well as other groups, invested and endured hardship in laying the foundations of our country. This helps explain why Anglophones (English speakers) are generally referred to as English Canadians.'
Anglophones came from England, Wales, Scotland, Ireland, plus other groups per p. 20.
Centuries-old origin per p. 20.
Not the explanation. p. 20 explains the historical settlement pattern.

en.question: Why did poets and songwriters hail Canada as 'the Great Dominion'?
options: Because Canadians had built a prosperous society from the Atlantic to the Pacific and Arctic
Because Canada had a large empire
en.explanation: Page 16: 'A belief in ordered liberty, enterprise, hard work and fair play have enabled Canadians to build a prosperous society in a rugged environment from our Atlantic shores to the Pacific Ocean and to the Arctic Circle — so much so that poets and songwriters have hailed Canada as the "Great Dominion."'

optionAnnotations.explanation: Page 16: 'A belief in ordered liberty, enterprise, hard work and fair play have enabled Canadians to build a prosperous society in a rugged environment from our Atlantic shores to the Pacific Ocean and to the Arctic Circle — so much so that poets and songwriters have hailed Canada as the "Great Dominion."'
Not the reason per p. 16. The 'Great Dominion' reference is about building prosperity coast to coast to coast.
Canada was not an empire; it was itself a Dominion within the British Empire.
Canada has a 'rugged environment' (p. 16) — far from tropical.
